title: What does a team share?
answer: Teammates share a life total, poison counters and turns. Hands, libraries, graveyards, mana pools, permanents and control remain separate.
explanation: Teammates share a life total, poison counters and turns. Hands, libraries, graveyards, mana pools, permanents and control remain separate.
example: An Island you tap produces mana in your pool. Your teammate cannot spend it to cast their spell.
exceptions: An effect can explicitly move resources or grant permissions; sharing a turn does not do that by itself.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Who are “you” and “each opponent”?
answer: “You” normally means the controller of the spell or ability. Your teammate is another player, but is not your opponent. Each opponent means both opposing players.
explanation: “You” normally means the controller of the spell or ability. Your teammate is another player, but is not your opponent. Each opponent means both opposing players.
example: A spell that makes each opponent lose 3 life causes two individual losses of 3: the opposing shared total falls by 6.
exceptions: A reference to your team does not merge control of cards.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does an extra turn give my teammate a turn too?
answer: Yes. An extra turn for one player becomes an extra turn for that player’s team. An extra phase or skipped step likewise applies to the team.
explanation: Yes. An extra turn for one player becomes an extra turn for that player’s team. An extra phase or skipped step likewise applies to the team.
example: Time Warp targeting you gives both teammates another shared turn.
exceptions: One effect giving both teammates an extra turn gives that team only one extra turn; separate effects can give multiple turns.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can one player skip the whole team’s draw or untap step?
answer: Yes. If an effect makes one teammate skip a step, the entire team skips that shared step.
explanation: Yes. If an effect makes one teammate skip a step, the entire team skips that shared step.
example: A player with Necropotence causes their team to skip its draw step. Neither teammate takes a normal draw in that step.
exceptions: Skipping a draw step is different from replacing one player’s individual draw.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: What are the life, commander-damage and poison thresholds?
answer: Commander Two-Headed Giant starts at 60 shared life. A team loses at 15 poison. Under CR 903.10a, a player dealt 21 combat damage by the same commander loses, causing their team to lose.
explanation: Commander Two-Headed Giant starts at 60 shared life. A team loses at 15 poison. Under CR 903.10a, a player dealt 21 combat damage by the same commander loses, causing their team to lose.
example: If one head has received 21 combat damage from one commander, their team loses even with life remaining. Yuriko’s life-loss trigger is not commander combat damage.
exceptions: The Wizards format overview uses team-level wording for commander damage; the CR tracks a recipient player. Aggregating damage split between heads is flagged for organizer clarification, not established here as a new league rule.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How do attacking and blocking work?
answer: The active team attacks together. Each attacker attacks a specified defending player, planeswalker or battle. Either defending teammate can block attacks against either head.
explanation: The active team attacks together. Each attacker attacks a specified defending player, planeswalker or battle. Either defending teammate can block attacks against either head.
example: Your teammate’s creature can block a creature attacking you. Unblocked damage is still attributed to the player actually attacked.
exceptions: Restrictions and costs are checked against the actual attack and the relevant defending player; a shared life total does not erase that choice.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can teammates use duplicate cards?
answer: Yes. Each Commander deck independently follows its size, singleton, commander and color-identity restrictions. Commander 2HG does not add a unified team singleton rule.
explanation: Yes. Each Commander deck independently follows its size, singleton, commander and color-identity restrictions. Commander 2HG does not add a unified team singleton rule.
example: Both decks can contain Sol Ring, provided each is legal in its own deck.
exceptions: This does not permit duplicate nonbasic cards within an individual deck unless a card or rule allows them.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does Silence protect a teammate’s winning turn?
answer: Silence stops both opponents from casting spells while your teammate can continue casting. Orim’s Chant stops only its target player from casting. If Chant was kicked, no creatures can attack that turn.
explanation: Silence stops both opponents from casting spells while your teammate can continue casting. Orim’s Chant stops only its target player from casting. If Chant was kicked, no creatures can attack that turn.
example: Player A casts Silence on the shared turn; after it resolves, player B can cast a winning spell. A kicked Chant also stops friendly attacks that turn.
exceptions: Neither removes spells already on the stack or generally stops activated or triggered abilities. Opponents can respond before the protection resolves.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Do Abolisher and Ranger-Captain cover both opponents?
answer: During your team’s turn, Grand Abolisher restricts both opponents. Ranger-Captain of Eos can stop both opponents from casting noncreature spells for the turn after its sacrifice ability resolves.
explanation: During your team’s turn, Grand Abolisher restricts both opponents. Ranger-Captain of Eos can stop both opponents from casting noncreature spells for the turn after its sacrifice ability resolves.
example: One teammate controls Abolisher while the other casts spells on their shared turn. Both enemies are opponents of Abolisher’s controller.
exceptions: Abolisher names activated abilities of artifacts, creatures and enchantments; it does not universally stop land or planeswalker abilities or triggered abilities. Ranger-Captain still allows creature spells.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can overloaded Rift or Winds hit my teammate?
answer: Yes. These overload effects affect qualifying permanents you do not control, including your teammate’s. Your teammate is not another part of “you.”
explanation: Yes. These overload effects affect qualifying permanents you do not control, including your teammate’s. Your teammate is not another part of “you.”
example: Overloaded Cyclonic Rift returns your teammate’s nonland permanents too. Overloaded Winds of Abandon exiles their creatures and lets their controller search for the lands it specifies.
exceptions: This differs from wording that explicitly affects opponents or permanents opponents control.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: What does Teferi’s Protection protect?
answer: Its life-total restriction keeps the shared life total from changing. Only its controller gets protection from everything, and only permanents that player controls phase out.
explanation: Its life-total restriction keeps the shared life total from changing. Only its controller gets protection from everything, and only permanents that player controls phase out.
example: Your teammate’s permanents stay on the battlefield. Damage to that teammate can still occur even though the shared life total cannot change.
exceptions: It does not generally prevent poison, commander combat-damage tracking or losing to an empty-library draw. Nonzero life payments cannot be made while the shared total cannot change.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: What does Sorin Markov’s −3 do to shared life?
answer: The targeted opponent’s team ends at 10 life if nothing modifies the change. Setting a player’s life total causes that player to gain or lose the difference, adjusting the shared total.
explanation: The targeted opponent’s team ends at 10 life if nothing modifies the change. Setting a player’s life total causes that player to gain or lose the difference, adjusting the shared total.
example: From 60, the targeted head loses 50, so the opposing team goes from 60 to 10. With your Bloodletter active on your turn, that 50 loss becomes 100, taking the team to −40.
exceptions: Life-loss replacements or prohibitions can change the result. Sorin targets an opponent, so it cannot target your teammate.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How do Pox and Bloodletter calculate life loss?
answer: Pox determines each player’s one-third loss from the shared total and rounds each loss up. Both heads lose that amount. Your Bloodletter doubles losses suffered by opponents during your team’s turn.
explanation: Pox determines each player’s one-third loss from the shared total and rounds each loss up. Both heads lose that amount. Your Bloodletter doubles losses suffered by opponents during your team’s turn.
example: At 60 each head loses 20: an unmodified team ends at 20. With your Bloodletter on your turn, each opposing head loses 40: the enemy team ends at −20. Your own team still ends at 20.
exceptions: Pox also discards and sacrifices; follow its whole resolution before state-based actions. Different starting totals and replacement effects change the arithmetic.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Test of Endurance or Felidar win from starting life?
answer: Yes, once their upkeep trigger can resolve with the required shared life total. Test of Endurance checks at least 50; Felidar Sovereign checks at least 40. A player’s win wins the team game.
explanation: Yes, once their upkeep trigger can resolve with the required shared life total. Test of Endurance checks at least 50; Felidar Sovereign checks at least 40. A player’s win wins the team game.
example: At 60 shared life, Test can trigger at its controller’s upkeep. If the team falls below 50 before it resolves, it will not win.
exceptions: These are intervening-if triggers: meet the threshold both at the start of upkeep and at resolution. A later life-gain trigger cannot create a missed win trigger.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does one Aetherflux Reservoir activation beat 60 life?
answer: Not by itself. Paying 50 from 60 leaves your team at 10. Dealing 50 to one opposing head takes an unmodified 60-life enemy team to 10.
explanation: Not by itself. Paying 50 from 60 leaves your team at 10. Dealing 50 to one opposing head takes an unmodified 60-life enemy team to 10.
example: From 60 versus 60, one activation leaves both teams at 10. A second activation requires enough life to pay another 50.
exceptions: Only spells Reservoir’s controller casts count toward its cast trigger. Damage prevention, life-gain restrictions and losing at zero can matter.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does my teammate gaining life trigger my life-gain cards?
answer: Not when they say “you gain life.” Life gain is attributed to an individual player even though it changes the shared total.
explanation: Not when they say “you gain life.” Life gain is attributed to an individual player even though it changes the shared total.
example: If your teammate gains 5, your Sanguine Bond does not trigger. If you gain 5, it does.
exceptions: A card explicitly watching a team or any player can work differently. Lifelink life gain goes to the source’s controller, not to whichever teammate needs a trigger.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How much shared life does Yuriko take?
answer: Each opponent loses life equal to the revealed card’s mana value, so the opposing team normally loses twice that value.
explanation: Each opponent loses life equal to the revealed card’s mana value, so the opposing team normally loses twice that value.
example: Revealing a mana-value-16 card causes each opponent to lose 16: 32 total from their shared life.
exceptions: This is life loss, not damage or commander combat damage. Putting the card into hand is not drawing it, so Narset’s draw limit does not stop that action.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can one teammate’s Aluren enable the other’s Acererak?
answer: Yes. Aluren gives every player its casting permission. Acererak’s controller can repeatedly cast and return their own Acererak while its Tomb of Annihilation condition permits.
explanation: Yes. Aluren gives every player its casting permission. Acererak’s controller can repeatedly cast and return their own Acererak while its Tomb of Annihilation condition permits.
example: Using Lost Mine of Phandelver, each Dark Pool visit drains each opponent for 1: 2 team life. Thirty visits remove 60 unmodified opposing life. Starting outside a dungeon, that path takes 119 Acererak entries and includes 29 mandatory Temple draws before the thirtieth Dark Pool.
exceptions: Requires Aluren, no completed Tomb, a usable dungeon path, enough library and no blocking restrictions or replacement effects. This is a conditional finite win line, not an unconditional infinite loop. Opponents also receive Aluren’s permission.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can a teammate’s Derevi help Najeela repeat combat?
answer: Derevi can untap a teammate’s mana permanent when Derevi’s controller’s creature deals combat damage to a player. Najeela’s controller can spend their own WUBRG to add a shared combat phase.
explanation: Derevi can untap a teammate’s mana permanent when Derevi’s controller’s creature deals combat damage to a player. Najeela’s controller can spend their own WUBRG to add a shared combat phase.
example: Player B connects with five of their creatures and uses five Derevi triggers to untap player A’s five suitable mana sources. A taps them to fund Najeela. Najeela untaps all attacking creatures, including B’s.
exceptions: The loop requires repeatable successful connections, the right colors and appropriate timing. Damage from A’s creatures does not trigger B’s Derevi. Mana is not pooled.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Do Sanguine Bond and Exquisite Blood loop across teammates?
answer: No. Shared life does not share life-gain events. Exquisite Blood makes its controller gain life; a teammate’s Sanguine Bond does not see that as “you” gaining life.
explanation: No. Shared life does not share life-gain events. Exquisite Blood makes its controller gain life; a teammate’s Sanguine Bond does not see that as “you” gaining life.
example: A controls Bond and B controls Blood. An opponent loses 1; B gains 1, raising the shared pool, but A’s Bond does not trigger.
exceptions: The familiar loop can work with both under the same controller, an initiating event and legal targets.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can we sacrifice artifacts together to Time Sieve?
answer: No. Time Sieve’s controller must sacrifice five artifacts they control. Teammates cannot contribute their own artifacts to that cost. A successful activation gives an extra team turn.
explanation: No. Time Sieve’s controller must sacrifice five artifacts they control. Teammates cannot contribute their own artifacts to that cost. A successful activation gives an extra team turn.
example: Three artifacts on A’s battlefield and two on B’s are not five artifacts A can sacrifice to A’s Sieve.
exceptions: Actual control-changing effects can alter which artifacts the activating player controls. A single extra turn does not prove a repeatable engine.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does teammate combat damage count for Tymna?
answer: Yes. Tymna counts opponents who were dealt combat damage this turn, regardless of which teammate’s creature dealt it. Ordinary life loss does not count.
explanation: Yes. Tymna counts opponents who were dealt combat damage this turn, regardless of which teammate’s creature dealt it. Ordinary life loss does not count.
example: If your teammate hits both opposing heads, your Tymna can let you pay 2 life and draw 2 at your postcombat main phase.
exceptions: Count distinct opposing players, at most two here, not creatures, hits, total life lost or damage to planeswalkers. You make the payment and draws.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How does Consecrated Sphinx see two opposing draws?
answer: Each opposing player’s draw triggers your Sphinx separately. During a normal enemy team draw step, two ordinary draws can produce two optional draw-two triggers.
explanation: Each opposing player’s draw triggers your Sphinx separately. During a normal enemy team draw step, two ordinary draws can produce two optional draw-two triggers.
example: Both opposing heads draw one card: you can draw four cards from the resulting two Sphinx triggers.
exceptions: Draws are ordered player by player under shared-turn rules, not a single shared draw. Draw replacement or skipping the step can reduce triggers. Only Sphinx’s controller draws.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How do Nekusar, Narset and Notion Thief interact?
answer: Nekusar adds a draw for each appropriate player and damages opponents for actual draws. Narset limits each enemy head separately. Notion Thief replaces qualifying opposing draws with draws for its own controller.
explanation: Nekusar adds a draw for each appropriate player and damages opponents for actual draws. Narset limits each enemy head separately. Notion Thief replaces qualifying opposing draws with draws for its own controller.
example: Normally the enemy heads each draw once normally and once from Nekusar: four total Nekusar damage. With your team’s Narset, each can draw at most one that turn. With Notion Thief, each first normal draw remains exempt, but additional draws can be stolen.
exceptions: A replaced draw is not an opponent drawing and does not trigger Nekusar for that opponent. Thief’s cards do not go to its teammate. Other replacement effects require separate analysis.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Rest in Peace and Helm work across teammates?
answer: Yes. Rest in Peace’s graveyard replacement is global. An allied Helm activation with X at least 1 can exile the targeted opponent’s library because no card actually enters that graveyard to meet Helm’s stopping condition.
explanation: Yes. Rest in Peace’s graveyard replacement is global. An allied Helm activation with X at least 1 can exile the targeted opponent’s library because no card actually enters that graveyard to meet Helm’s stopping condition.
example: A controls Rest in Peace. B activates their Helm for X=1 targeting an opposing head. That head’s library is exiled.
exceptions: Exiling the library is not itself a win: the opponent must attempt a draw from it, or lose another way. Replacement conflicts, removing Rest in Peace or stopping the activation can break the line.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does my Kinnan boost my teammate’s Basalt Monolith?
answer: No. Kinnan triggers when you tap a nonland permanent for mana. A teammate tapping their Basalt is not you tapping it.
explanation: No. Kinnan triggers when you tap a nonland permanent for mana. A teammate tapping their Basalt is not you tapping it.
example: A controls Kinnan; B taps Basalt for 3 and pays 3 to untap it. A’s Kinnan adds no mana, so this does not generate surplus mana.
exceptions: With Kinnan and Basalt under the same controller, their mana interaction is different. It still does not transfer mana to an ally.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How many extra turns can Expropriate produce?
answer: Each of the four players votes separately. Each time vote creates a separate extra turn for Expropriate’s controller, and each becomes an extra team turn.
explanation: Each of the four players votes separately. Each time vote creates a separate extra turn for Expropriate’s controller, and each becomes an extra team turn.
example: If you and your teammate both vote time and both opponents vote money, your team gets two extra turns. For each money voter you choose a permanent they own and gain control of it; that permanent can be a land.
exceptions: Votes are not pooled by team. Money uses ownership, not merely who currently controls a permanent. The spell is exiled and is not intrinsically a repeatable-turn engine.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Do Contamination and Collector Ouphe affect allies?
answer: Yes. Contamination modifies lands tapped for mana regardless of controller; Collector Ouphe stops activated abilities of everyone’s artifacts, including mana abilities.
explanation: Yes. Contamination modifies lands tapped for mana regardless of controller; Collector Ouphe stops activated abilities of everyone’s artifacts, including mana abilities.
example: With Contamination active, even an ally’s multi-mana land produces one black instead. With Ouphe active, an ally cannot activate Basalt Monolith’s mana or untap ability.
exceptions: Contamination’s upkeep sacrifice must be a creature its controller controls. Ouphe does not prohibit casting artifact spells or stop triggered abilities.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can K’rrik or Citadel spend the shared 60 life?
answer: Yes. Your life payments come from the shared total. The spell or ability and its benefits still belong to the player using it.
explanation: Yes. Your life payments come from the shared total. The spell or ability and its benefits still belong to the player using it.
example: K’rrik’s controller can pay 2 life for an eligible black mana symbol, reducing their team’s shared total by 2. Their teammate cannot make that payment in their place.
exceptions: A legal payment must be affordable. Paying down to zero normally loses the team the game at the next state-based check; life-change restrictions can forbid payment.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Do Children of Korlis refund my teammate’s life payments?
answer: No. Children counts life its controller personally lost this turn, not all decreases to the team pool.
explanation: No. Children counts life its controller personally lost this turn, not all decreases to the team pool.
example: A pays 20 life using their own spells. B sacrifices Children: B does not gain 20 merely because the shared total fell.
exceptions: If an effect caused B to lose life too, B counts that actual loss, even if other gains have since raised the team pool.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can allied Heliod and Walking Ballista sustain the loop?
answer: Not merely by splitting the pieces. Heliod triggers on its controller’s life gain and can put counters only on creatures or enchantments that player controls.
explanation: Not merely by splitting the pieces. Heliod triggers on its controller’s life gain and can put counters only on creatures or enchantments that player controls.
example: A’s Heliod gives B’s Ballista lifelink. Ballista’s damage makes B gain life, so A’s Heliod does not trigger; A also cannot use its counter trigger on B’s Ballista.
exceptions: Targeting another creature with Heliod’s lifelink activation can include a teammate’s creature. That permission does not share the resulting triggers.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: How does Gray Merchant scale against two opponents?
answer: Count only its controller’s devotion to black. Each opposing head loses that much life, and that controller gains the total actually lost.
explanation: Count only its controller’s devotion to black. Each opposing head loses that much life, and that controller gains the total actually lost.
example: At devotion 8, each opponent loses 8: the enemy pool falls by 16 and Gray Merchant’s controller gains 16.
exceptions: An ally’s black permanents do not add devotion. Prevention or replacement of loss can change how much life is gained.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does Havoc Festival halve the team twice?
answer: Yes, its “that player” upkeep triggers apply to each active head. The triggers resolve separately, recalculating the shared total for each half-loss.
explanation: Yes, its “that player” upkeep triggers apply to each active head. The triggers resolve separately, recalculating the shared total for each half-loss.
example: At 60 on the affected team’s upkeep: first trigger loses 30, leaving 30; second loses 15, leaving 15. It does not simultaneously subtract 30 twice.
exceptions: Each loss rounds up from the current shared total. The no-life-gain effect affects everyone.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Heartless Hidetsugu eliminate both teams?
answer: Its one ability damages every player based on half their team’s current life, rounded down. Both heads’ damage reduces the same team total.
explanation: Its one ability damages every player based on half their team’s current life, rounded down. Both heads’ damage reduces the same team total.
example: At 60, each head takes 30: that team reaches 0. At 61, each takes 30: it reaches 1. With both teams at 60 and no modifying effects, the simultaneous losses make the game a draw.
exceptions: Damage prevention, replacement effects, immunity to losing and damage multipliers change this result. Do not assume a safe unilateral win.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does Repay in Kind apply the life reduction twice per team?
answer: No. When one effect sets both teammates’ life totals to a number, the team chooses one teammate to be affected.
explanation: No. When one effect sets both teammates’ life totals to a number, the team chooses one teammate to be affected.
example: With teams at 60 and 20, Repay in Kind makes the 60-life team become 20, not −20. The other remains at 20.
exceptions: This differs from an effect making each player lose an amount of life, such as Pox.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Is Serra Ascendant active at 60 starting life?
answer: Yes. Its threshold is a fixed 30 life, so a 60-life team satisfies it.
explanation: Yes. Its threshold is a fixed 30 life, so a 60-life team satisfies it.
example: Its base 1/1 becomes a 6/6 with flying while the team is at least 30; its lifelink gains life for its controller.
exceptions: It does not require 30 more than starting life. Falling below 30 removes that bonus.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: What does doubling one head’s life do?
answer: Beacon of Immortality doubles the shared total by causing its targeted player to gain the difference.
explanation: Beacon of Immortality doubles the shared total by causing its targeted player to gain the difference.
example: Targeting one head on a 60-life team makes that head gain 60, raising the pool to 120. Only that head’s “you gain life” abilities see that event.
exceptions: Gain restrictions and replacement effects can alter or prevent the increase. The spell can target a teammate or opponent.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does one Platinum Angel protect the whole team from losing?
answer: Yes. If a player cannot lose, their team cannot lose. If a player cannot win, their team cannot win.
explanation: Yes. If a player cannot lose, their team cannot lose. If a player cannot win, their team cannot win.
example: One teammate’s Platinum Angel can keep the team from losing at zero life while its ability remains active.
exceptions: It does not stop damage, remove poison or restore libraries. Removing or disabling the effect can expose accumulated loss conditions.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Do The One Ring or Glacial Chasm shield my teammate?
answer: No. Their controller-specific protection or damage prevention is not shared with the other head. Unlike Teferi’s Protection, these effects do not freeze the shared life total.
explanation: No. Their controller-specific protection or damage prevention is not shared with the other head. Unlike Teferi’s Protection, these effects do not freeze the shared life total.
example: An enemy can attack the unprotected teammate and reduce the shared pool even while you have The One Ring’s protection.
exceptions: Glacial Chasm restricts its controller’s creatures from attacking and requires that player’s cumulative-upkeep life payments; it does not stop an ally’s attacks.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Does proliferating both heads add two poison counters?
answer: No. If both teammates are chosen, their team gets only one additional poison counter. The proliferating player chooses which head receives it.
explanation: No. If both teammates are chosen, their team gets only one additional poison counter. The proliferating player chooses which head receives it.
example: An opposing team with 14 poison reaches 15 from a proliferate effect, not 16 by choosing both heads.
exceptions: A team must already have a poison counter for proliferation to add one. Poison dealt separately by sources is a different event.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Earthcraft untap my teammate’s land?
answer: Yes, if it is a basic land. The creature tapped as the cost must be yours; the target basic land can belong to a teammate.
explanation: Yes, if it is a basic land. The creature tapped as the cost must be yours; the target basic land can belong to a teammate.
example: A taps their creature for Earthcraft to untap B’s basic Island. B can then tap that Island for mana in B’s own pool.
exceptions: This does not transfer mana. Earthcraft’s cost is not a creature’s own tap-symbol ability, so summoning sickness does not prohibit that cost.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Arcum convert my teammate’s artifact creature?
answer: Yes. Arcum can target any artifact creature. That creature’s controller sacrifices it and may search their own library for the specified noncreature artifact.
explanation: Yes. Arcum can target any artifact creature. That creature’s controller sacrifices it and may search their own library for the specified noncreature artifact.
example: A activates Arcum targeting B’s artifact creature. B sacrifices it, searches B’s library and puts B’s artifact onto the battlefield.
exceptions: A pays Arcum’s activation cost. The target must remain legal; a player cannot sacrifice a permanent they do not control.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can I equip a teammate, and who gets Sword triggers?
answer: Ordinary equip targets only a creature you control. If an equipped creature later changes controller, equipment and creature can have different controllers. Triggers belonging to the Equipment still belong to its controller.
explanation: Ordinary equip targets only a creature you control. If an equipped creature later changes controller, equipment and creature can have different controllers. Triggers belonging to the Equipment still belong to its controller.
example: With A’s Sword of Feast and Famine attached to a creature now controlled by B, the Sword trigger untaps A’s lands. An ability granted to a creature, such as Bear Umbra’s attack ability, is controlled through that creature instead.
exceptions: Changing control does not itself move Equipment. Other attachment effects may allow targets ordinary equip does not.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Duelist’s Heritage or Bruse boost allied attackers?
answer: Duelist’s Heritage can target an attacking creature controlled by your teammate. Bruse Tarl’s trigger specifically targets a creature you control.
explanation: Duelist’s Heritage can target an attacking creature controlled by your teammate. Bruse Tarl’s trigger specifically targets a creature you control.
example: A’s Heritage can grant double strike to B’s attacker; A’s Bruse trigger cannot target it.
exceptions: Each ability’s actual targeting restriction governs. A shared combat phase does not share control.
change_note: Initial source-checked reference; interpretations are worked examples, not new Wizards rulings.

title: Can Mindcrank and Bloodchief Ascension work across teammates?
